section_1.title: Intuitive Hook: The 'Moving Window' Concept
section_1.content: Define convolution as a sliding window operation. Introduce the input signal (a 1D array or 2D image) and the 'Kernel' (a smaller matrix that acts as a filter). Explain the process of element-wise multiplication and summation.
section_1.example: Imagine a 3x3 'blurring window' sliding over a pixelated photo of a cat; the output pixel is the average of the window's current view.

section_2.title: Mathematical Mechanics (The Sliding Dot Product)
section_2.content: Briefly define the mathematical notation: (f * g)[n] = Σ f[m]g[n-m]. Emphasize the 'flip and shift' nature of the operation. Use a visual animation where the kernel flips horizontally and slides across the input sequence.
section_2.example: A 1D audio signal spike being smoothed by a simple [0.5, 0.5] kernel, effectively averaging two adjacent audio samples.

section_3.title: Visualizing Operations: Filters as Feature Detectors
section_3.content: Explain how different kernels extract different information. Contrast an 'Identity' kernel (no change) with an 'Edge Detection' kernel (highlights intensity jumps). Show how the kernel acts as a 'search pattern' for specific local features.
section_3.example: A kernel designed to look like a vertical line will produce a high value (bright spot) only when it passes over a vertical stripe on a cartoon character.

section_4.title: Real-World Application: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
section_4.content: Connect the concept to modern AI. Explain that in Deep Learning, these kernels are 'learned' rather than predefined. The computer automatically figures out which filters best identify features like eyes, ears, or whiskers.
section_4.example: How an AI model detects a 'dog' by stacking multiple convolution layers: first finding edges, then textures, and finally entire facial shapes.

section_5.title: Summary and Synthesis
section_5.content: Recap the progression: From a simple local operation (sliding) to complex feature extraction (AI). Emphasize that convolution is the core 'lens' through which computers perceive the physical world.
section_5.example: A concluding animation of a robot's perspective: an input frame of a human face transforming into a set of 'activated' feature maps through sequential convolutions.

class TeachingScene(Scene):

                           "We flip and shift the kernel across.",

section_1.content: Define convolution as a sliding window operation. Introduce the input signal (a 1D array or 2D image) and the 'Kernel' (a smaller matrix that acts as a filter). Explain the process of element-wise multiplication and summation.
section_1.example: Imagine a 3x3 'blurring window' sliding over a pixelated photo of a cat; the output pixel is the average of the window's current view.

section_2.title: Mathematical Mechanics (The Sliding Dot Product)
section_2.content: Briefly define the mathematical notation: (f * g)[n] = Σ f[m]g[n-m]. Emphasize the 'flip and shift' nature of the operation. Use a visual animation where the kernel flips horizontally and slides across the input sequence.
section_2.example: A 1D audio signal spike being smoothed by a simple [0.5, 0.5] kernel, effectively averaging two adjacent audio samples.

section_3.title: Visualizing Operations: Filters as Feature Detectors
section_3.content: Explain how different kernels extract different information. Contrast an 'Identity' kernel (no change) with an 'Edge Detection' kernel (highlights intensity jumps). Show how the kernel acts as a 'search pattern' for specific local features.
section_3.example: A kernel designed to look like a vertical line will produce a high value (bright spot) only when it passes over a vertical stripe on a cartoon character.

section_4.title: Real-World Application: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
section_4.content: Connect the concept to modern AI. Explain that in Deep Learning, these kernels are 'learned' rather than predefined. The computer automatically figures out which filters best identify features like eyes, ears, or whiskers.
section_4.example: How an AI model detects a 'dog' by stacking multiple convolution layers: first finding edges, then textures, and finally entire facial shapes.

section_5.title: Summary and Synthesis
section_5.content: Recap the progression: From a simple local operation (sliding) to complex feature extraction (AI). Emphasize that convolution is the core 'lens' through which computers perceive the physical world.
section_5.example: A concluding animation of a robot's perspective: an input frame of a human face transforming into a set of 'activated' feature maps through sequential convolutions.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)

        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
